title: Research Methods 1
text:
Introduction
This page provides the course materials for BEEM136, the Research Methods 1 course at the University of Exeter. This course is designed to accompany you as you conduct your own research in economics. This course has a particular focus on empirical projects, with a micro-economics flavour. Nonetheless, I hope many of the research tools discussed will be useful regardless of the precise nature of the research you conduct.
Throughout this course we will cover the following topics:

An introduction to Various Statistical Programming Languages
Further information on Data Wrangling and Data Management
Information Related to Research Project Management
Further Information on Data Visualisation and Graphics
A Discussion of Statistical Tools and the Generation of Tables
A Discussion of Simulation and Econometrics
Some Further Useful Tools such as git/gitub, LaTeX, websraping

Precise details about the nature of the course are found on the following page.
Welcome!

title: About This Course
text:
Background Information
This course seeks to provide you with a base for your research in economics. In particular, the focus of this course will be on computational methods which are frequently used in economic research. We will be working with scientific programming languages, and discussing themes relevant to conducting research. The goal of this course is that by the end, you will have knowledge of the computation tools necessary to embark on a serious research project in economics, such as a paper or a thesis.
This course is in some sense language-neutral, and I will ask that each of you work with a language that you have never worked with before. In the early portions of the course, information will be provided on a number of languages, and then we will provide instruction in particular in R, Python and Stata. In later parts of the course, we will rotate, considering particular themes in one of these languages, where the focus will be on the substance of the theme, rather than the particular syntax of the language. In this portion of the course, if you have chosen to work in another language, the idea is that you can work on the same these, however in your chosen language. In Tutorials, at one point during the semester, I will request if each one of you could demonstrate to the class how to apply the week’s methods in the language that you have chosen to work with. If, however, you would like to work in another language apart from R, Python or Stata, please let me know, to confirm that this will work.
The only restriction here is that I am requesting that each person start working in a language that they do not have prior experience in. I am doing this for two reasons. The first is that this way we will all start with the same level (none) of language specific knowledge on the particular language we are working in. The second is that in this way, at the end of the semester you will each have knowledge of an entirely new language that may open more doors for you later on. If you have no experience at all programming in the past this is entirely fine. Indeed, I will start this class with the assumption that you have no background knowledge, and so anything that you do know is only a bonus for you (and the class).
The principal resource of this course will be this website which will provide notes, code and code output. A pdf or epub version of these notes can be downloaded at top left-hand corner of the page, though generally presentation is optimised for the website. The site will be updated section-by-section, with each section of the notes going live on the day the class will be given. These resources will then be available on the website for the entire semester. I would encourage you to attend classes in person where ever possible!

title: About This Course
text:
Evaluation
The evaluation of this course will consist of the following two elements:

Ongoing assessment (20%): Tutorial presentation (please sign up for your desired slot).
An Empirical Project (80%): Full details provided around week 3 of term. Hand in date is at the end of semester.

Full details on these evaluations will be made available below in line with the dates in the calendar.






Tutorial Presentation



For this evaluation, I will ask you to prepare an example of code for us to work through in the tutorial slot together. The idea of this presentation is that you will show us how to do something that we saw in class, however apply it to the language that you are working with. Thus, the date you present will depend on the language that you decide to work in. The only restriction here is that I will ask you not to present about a specific theme if we have already seen this theme in that language in classes with me. Please refer to the “Language” column in the proposed schedule to ensure that this does not occur.
For this presentation I will ask that you generate an example along the lines of the themes we have seen in class the week before. So, for example, if you wish to present on data management and cleaning and are not working in Stata, you may wish to show us an example of joining some data bases and cleaning particular variables in the language that you are working with. Or if you would like present about data visualisation and graphics and are not working in Python, you may wish to show us how to make some particularly nice graph using real data of interest to you in the language that you are working with.
I would ask that you prepare an example that will take about 10-15 minutes to explain. 10-15 minutes may sound like a long presentation, but when you are explaining your code and the goal of your analysis, it is probably less than you think. You may wish to simply work with code and output in the program that you are working with, or generate some set of slides along side of the code that you will work with in class. I would ask that you show us how the code runs on your computer or on the screen, so that we can look into particular lines of code together. If your presentation generates discussion or extensions and goes for more than 10-15 minutes this is perfectly fine. We will have the entire tutorial block to discuss these examples, and any questions which come up as a result.
Please confirm a date with me and I will include the date for your presentation in the calendar above. Please also feel free to discuss with me the precise themes that we will work with each week if you want to set-up your presentation a few weeks in advance.








Empirical Project



At the end of the semester, please hand in an empirical project. This empirical project is expected to cover the themes discussed in the course, and can be on a topic of your choosing. You should view this empirical project as a mini research project. However what is important in this project is not the results per se but rather the process you follow in bringing everything together.
Some potential ideas of projects could be things such as:

Find a paper of interest to you and aim to replicate the question (in a limited way) in another setting
Replicate and extend a paper using the data provided by the authors*
Examine a number of papers on a similar topic and document how methods and codes vary across papers
Find data about some topic of interest to you and run a mini-analysis. In this case, what is important is not empirical design, but rather the process you follow in setting up your project.
Write and document some package which can extend the functionality of Python, R or Stata
* If you choose to replicate a paper, it is not sufficient to simply show that it replicates. The idea is that you should extend the analysis, ideally with further data.

You should not feel like this is the limit of what you can do. If you would like to do alternative things that can be conceived to be an research project, this is great, and please just confirm your intentions with me.
If you wish to check with me about what you propose to do for your empirical project, feel free to ask me or write me at any time! I would encourage you to do so at some point during the term when you start to get an idea of what you would like to do for this project.
Please hand in all the materials you used for your project in a single organised zipped folder (.zip or .7z), or pdf pointing to a github repo or similar. Please hand this in via the submission point on the ELE page of this course no later than 11:59am on Monday 12th of January, 2025. What you hand in will depend a bit on the nature of your project, but at a minimum your materials should consist of:

All data and code
a README file explaining how to replicate everything you have done
A compiled pdf containing sections including: Introduction, Data, Methods, Results, and Conclusion. This pdf should not exceed 15 pages. If you wish to include appendix results this is fine, and will not count towards the 15 pages.

The evaluation of the project will consider the elements below. The “proportion” refers to the approximate importance that these elements will be given in the final mark. The final mark will consist of an overall grade along with written comments from me, but will not provide an itemised break down, and as such the elements below are simply to help you ensure that your project touches on all relevant components. Marking will follow the typical system used in the MRes where 50 or above is a pass, 70 or above signifies excellent work (ie a level of first class honours), and 80 signifies something truly outstanding.

General Comment

There is no single “correct” way for this to be done, and it depends on exactly what your project is like. If, however, you are applying the tools of the class to some particular research question of interest (such as the fourth bullet point of the list at the top of this description), I would suggest that you should hand in a pdf structured as follows:

Introduction - Around 1-3 pages, noting the context you are looking at, explain what you do, citing some key literature and the motivation (somewhat similar to a short version of the introduction of a standard economic paper)
Data - Around 2-5 pages, explaining fully the data you use, any cleaning done, any other information useful for readers, and providing full summary statistics and relevant descriptives
Methods - Around 1-2 page, explain simply what you will do, laying out any estimating equations. Here you could also include information related to weighting of models (if relevant), or other key methodological points
Results - Around 2-6 pages, providing any results you produce which may be tables, graphs, and so forth. Explain to me what you find, and the implications of this, noting any key limitations
Conclusion - Around 1 page, simply summarising what you have found, any key take-aways, key limitations, and future work that may be motivated by this project
Bibliography

Please note, the above description may not correspond exactly to what you are doing, and so should be viewed as simply one particular way that this could be addressed, rather than a prescriptive list which must be followed. Please talk to me if you would like to discuss what you are doing, or get any interim feedback!

title: Background on Computational Languages in Economics
text:
Computer Languages in Economics
A range of computer languages are currently in use in economics, and in your own reasearch career, if you are conducting empirical research, it is likely that you will use a number of languages. What we will spend most of our time working on in this course are languages with scientific programming capacities. These languages will generally be designed to – or have certain aspects designed to – work with data, conduct numerical calculations, and, ideally, have a set of inbuilt statistical routines which we frequently encounter in economics. Ideally, as well as allowing us to conduct our research, the languages we work with will allow us to generate the types of exhibits we would like to communicate our research with our peers: things like tables and figures.
In modern economic practice, I believe that the most frequently used statistical programming languages (in alphabeticl order) are Julia, Matlab, Python, R and Stata. Among these, Julia is newer and less adopted, but may take off in the years ahead. This is not to say that you will not encounter other languages in your career. Other languages are indeed used. For example, many old structural models are written in Fortran, and certain sub-fields in economics may use other languages such as SAS, OxMetrix, Mathematica, SPSS and other tools.
One may ask why so many languages exist? Languages are designed with different philosophies, and often new languages are developed to remedy perceived shortcomings of older languages. Originally, computer languages were low level. Low level languages are computational languages which require the programmer to think carefully about how the program they write interacts with a computer’s memory, and are generally more complex to write, but faster to run. Currently, all of the languages frequently used in economic research are high level. High level languages are written to take care of things like memory and hardware use, garbage collection, assignment of variable types and so forth, and so the programmer can simply focus on the task at hand. High level languages are generally faster to program in, but codes run more slowly. This is an “abstraction penalty” with moving to higher level coding – more is taken care of, but some cost is generally paid in terms of computing time. To see below the example of what the difference can look like between more low level and high level languages, refer to the following two codes to print “Hello World!” on the computer screen. The left-hand side is the code for Python, while the right-hand side is the code for C. Over time this movement from low to high level has implied a number of new languages have been developed.
Another key reason why multiple languages exist is that some languages are written by companies to be sold, while other are written to be open source and increase access to scientific tools without payment. Commercial languages are produced with paid developers, and generally offer high quality documentation and warranties on performance. However, large open source languages have many active contributers (working on a voluntary basis), and so are often able to match or exceed the performance of commercial languages, especially when it comes to rapidly incorporating new advances into their code base.
Finally, different languages generally have different focuses. For example, among the languages we will work with in this course, Stata is most focused on rapidly being able to work with data and perform statistical analyses, R has a somewhat similar focus but is open source, Python provides more control over a computer’s entire operating system, and certain other languages such as Matlab are designed specifically for matrix-based calculations (which are extremely frequent in economics). In general, languages will have specific design choices, and when you work with one or another they will have a different feel. A key distinction which we will see throughout the course is in how they deal with repeated calculations or processes. Certain languages are more structured to conduct repeated calculations in sequence, essentially “looping” around and doing one thing after another, while others are more structured to think in terms of matrices, applying a process in block to many cells of a matrix.
Some of the distinctions between languages which you may encounter are summarised in the Table below. Many of these categorisations are just my perception. For example, all computer languages are “fast” in that they can perform millions of calculations per second, but in my experience some or faster than others, and this may be relevant if you end up working on very computationally intensive projects. If you are interested in some more formal comparisons of languages, you may wish to read the paper by (Aruoba2015?) .

+ Certain elements are optimized for matricial calculations (Mata)

title: Background on Computational Languages in Economics
section: Considerations in Adopting a New Language
text:
Considerations in Adopting a New Language
When you are learning a new programming language, many of the things you learn will be general knowledge that will also help you in other languages. For example, certain programming constructs such as the use of formal logic, control flow statements such as loops, the generation of functions and so forth will be something you encounter in nearly any language. However, there is also a non-trivial investment in language specific factors, for example the syntax of the language (the way the language is written and used), as well as the use of particular commands, will not cross over from language to language. For this reason, it is worth thinking about which is the best language for you prior to starting.
Generically, there is no right answer to this question as it depends on what you do and your own prefernces. There are, however, a number of considerations which I believe can help you decide which programming language is right for you. Among other things, relevant factors to consider include the following:

What type of research will I be doing?
Are there any relevant network effects (for example coauthors)?
What is my current knowledge?
What type of support do I look for?
Do I have any deeper preferences to satisfy?

I will discuss these points briefly below.

1. What type of research will I be doing?
There are certain types of research where specific languags may be especially well suited to what you are doing. For example, if you plan to be largely working with and cleaning data and performing econometric analyses, you could conceivably work with Julia, R, Python or Stata (among others). However, Stata or R might be the most logical choices, because often these are the first place where new econometric routines turn up. Often econometricians or other applied reseachers release new tools in Stata or in R first, and then only later do they appear in other languages.
If, however, you plan to be working with more modern machine learning (ML) tools, Python or R are probably leaders here. While ML routines are also certainly available in Stata and Julia (among others), at the moment my feeling is that they are most well developed in R and Python, as they are often contributed by non-economists.
You may have other preferences, for example your research may involve solving formal optimisation problems, for example in structural work. In this case, the optimisation routines in Matlab may be particularly relevant. Julia may catch up to Matlab with optimisation routines, though at the moment my feeling is that Matlab is still the leader here.
One useful way to have an idea about the types of codes that might be relevant in particular research projects is to look at the replication materials that are available with papers that you read. If you see that they all are using a certain language, this may be a useful insight for you. One thing to note with this is that historically, much of the code base in economics has been written in Stata, so it is likely that this will feature heavily in many fields.


2. Are there any relevant network effects?
A highly relevant consideration in many cases is the need to interact with coauthors, supervisors, and so forth. Often, our decision about the language we use may be largely driven by the people we work with. For example, if all of my coauthors use one language and want to be involved in programming in a paper, it makes sense for me to also work in that language. Or if part of a paper is already written by another coauthor in a particular language, it may make sense to continue working in this language to ease the work flow involved in the project.
As mentioned above, historically a lot of work in economics has been conducted in Stata, and the network effects from this have meant that Stata remains highly relevant. It seems to me that more recently there is some broadening of the scope of languages used, and you should of course feel free to not be guided by what others do to make your choice. The relevance of network effects will probably be most relevant if you plan to be frequently involved in collaborative projects.


3. What is my current knowledge?
You may already know a programming language and feel comfortable in it. In this course, I will ask that you all work with a programming language that you have not worked with before, and we will discuss a range of languages thoughout the course. The reason for this is that this way it is guaranteed that we will all start at a reasonably similar base (even if people have never programmed before), and at the end of the course you will at least feel comfortable in a new programming language. Often the spillovers from one language to the next will depend a little bit on their structure. For example, if you have worked before with a matrix-oriented language such as Matlab, you may wish to work in R which has something of a similar logic. However, if you have experience in Python and like the idea of looping, Stata may be a more logical choice in terms of a new syntax.


4. What type of support do I look for?
A fourth point to consider is related to the support you want in your work. In the section below we will discuss more fully the types of support available for different languages, and this definitely depends a lot on the language. Certain languages have dedicated and extremely active forums where you can ask questions, and get feedback. Languages also differ in terms of the degree of quality of the manuals, the activity level of people in online forums, and the quality of responses in online forums. Another relevant point in this dimension is how well the languages are supported in large language models like ChatGPT. This will be discussed at more length below.
At present, my subjective opinion is that if we consider the languages Stata, Python, R and Julia, the ordering of support depends highly upon what type of support one seeks. In terms of quality of manuals, the ordering is probably something like – from best to worst – (1) Stata (2) R (3) Python and Julia. However in terms of support from ChatGPT it is probably (1) Python (2) R (3) Julia (4) Stata. And in terms of forums, specifically for relatively new users, the support available is probably ordered as (1) Stata (2) Python and R (3) Julia.


5. Do I have any deeper preferences to satisfy?
Finally, you may have deeper preferences. For example, you may appreciate the value of Open Source software, and prefer to opt for open source tools. A surprising amount of the current technological world is built with or on top of the contributions of open source software (see the comic below!), and you may wish to be part of this. You may also have other preferences which are relevant for you at the moment you decide.

title: Background on Computational Languages in Economics
section: How Should I Learn a New Language?
text:
How Should I Learn a New Language?
There are a number of tools which can help you in learning a new language, but by far, the most useful way to learning a programming language is by programming in it! Right at the beginning, it is useful to understand the minimum basic elements of the language, which is what we will focus on immediately after this section of the course. At all points, my suggestion would be to put in practice what you are learning, working with examples which are interesting to you. Personally, I would not endorse trying to perfect your knowledge of a language in theory before you put it into practice. Once you have a basic understanding of the language, in my opinion, the best thing you can do is to start working in it, and learn the particular things you need in your everyday usage by trying to do particular things of interest, for example generate graphs, examine data, and so forth.
There is an important caveats here, and this is that I would certainly not endorse using a language for a real paper before you are sure that you understand the key elements. There are certain elements of research projects which are critical, for example cleaning and joining data, and if done incorrectly can mean that your final results are entirely wrong. We will discuss these elements at more length later in the course, but for now it is worth keeping in mind that while learning by doing is an efficient way to figure out how a language works and how it doesn’t work, when you are dealing with real programs, it is important to build in checks throughout your work to ensure that you aren’t making mistakes. We will discuss this a little later in the course.
Beyond learnign by doing, there are a number of highly useful resources online that will help you get up to speed. We discuss these below.

Online Forums
A hugely useful source of information are online forums which let you ask questions, and suggest answers to questions if you know about a particular language. The most common forum is Stack Overflow where you can generate an account and ask questions about any language. These questions are often answered within minutes, and multiple responses can be provided, with individuals voting to highlight best answers. As well as a place to answer your own qustions, Stack Overflow is a hugely relevant resource to search for previous responses. Frequently, questions you may have are already answered on Stack Overflow, and can be found by searching Stack overflow or by using a search engine.
For certain languages, alternative forums exist. For example, the Statalist in the case of Stata has a much richer set of questions and answers than Stack overflow. This would be my first port of call for Stata-related queries, with the many questions already answered in the archives of the list. This can also be searched quite simply prior to asking a new question, and a well-established etiquette exists see here, for example.


Large Language Models
More and more, large language models (LLMs) like chatGPT and other Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools can help us with our programming tasks. Certain platforms also have AIs which can help you in developing your code, such as github’s copilot. If you are unsure of certain language constructs, using an LLM can be very helpful, though it is also important to generate your own understanding of the language alongside inputs from LLMs. It is also relevant to note that the quality of responses from LLMs will depend slightly upon the amount of data they have to learn from, though in general for most languages we encounter LLMs are do a good job.
My personal view is that you should avoid using these LLMs as a crutch. For the large majority of types of programming we will be doing in economic research, we will not want to be relying on vibe coding, nor outsourcing the thinking to LLMs. Of course, LLMs can help increase productivity and offer suggestions for ways to optimise code. Things like line completion in VS code and other constructs can be very helpful to speed up programming, but we must be vigilant in ensuring that we’re getting what we actually want. Actually learning how to programme the old fashioned way and knowing syntax off by heart offers considerable benefits in terms of understanding code, as well as more generally getting a feel for different programming constructs. It’s also useful for when you want to programme when you’re on the road with less access to wifi, or in settings without access to internet, such as data rooms maintained by governmental data providers.

title: Background on Computational Languages in Economics
text:
Hardware and Operating Systems
While this course is focused on learning a scientific computing languages for research in economics, it is useful for you to have some understanding of the hardware you use, as well as make an informed choice about operating systems. While generally, current laptops have remarkable processing capacity, for certain types of projects you may run into bottlenecks either in terms of memory or processing power.

Hardware
Broadly speaking, and at a very high level of abstraction, there will be three particularly relevant elements for us when thinking about the hardware we use. The first is the processing capacity of the computer, which depends upon the Central Processing Unit, or CPU. The second is the virtual memory capacity the computer has to manipulate specific data bases, which depends upon the Random Access Memory, or RAM. And the last is the hard disk space and the type of hard disk used to store all of the data and programmes installed on the computer.
We will not discuss this in great depth, but it is useful to note that particular types of projects will imply demands on particular types of resources, and if you are deciding on what type of computer you need, this will be driven by the type of research you are doing. For example, if you are doing research which is particularly demanding in terms of numerical processing or in terms of calculations, the most important thing that you will want to consider will be the type and number of CPUs that you have. More recent generations of CPUs have greater processing capacities1 In extremely demanding projects where processing capacity is a limiting constraint, processing can even be done on the Graphical Processing Unit, or GPU, of your computer, though this is likely not relevant for the majority of projects in economics, so we won’t dig into it here. If, however, your research requires working with large databases, for example running regressions with many millions of operations, it is more likely that your bottleneck will be in terms of RAM. Given that you need enough RAM to hold databases in working memory, if you plan to work with databases of >16GB for example, you will require a machine with more than 16GB of RAM. Finally, though potentially less limiting, is the relevance of the hard disk. If you plan to store massive amounts of data on your computer (of the order of terrabytes), you may find that you run out of hard disk space. In general this is relatively easy to remedy by purchasing an external hard drive, but is also a choice which can be made when deciding on a computer to use.


Operating Systems
The operating system is the over-arching environment where we interact with all our programs, data management, and so forth. It is extremely likely that you will work with some flavour of Windows, OS, or Unix-based operating systems. Often, operating systems are bundled with hardware, and when you purchase your computer this choice will be made.
The simplicity with which you are able to program does vary by the operating system you choose. In my opinion, Unix based operating systems are by far the most flexible and most well-suited to scientific computing. However, there is a learning curve involved in getting up to speed with a new OS, and you may not wish to do this. Regardless of the choice of OS you make, all the tools we examine in the course will be available, and more generally, nearly all the computational tools you will require in economics can be somehow made to work on each type of OS.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
R
In the following section, we will provide a primer to number of languages, specifically R, Python and Stata. These introduction seek to provide the necessary tools to get up and running with the things that we will need throughout the rest of the course, but are not desiged to be comprehensive overviews of the entirety of each language. We will further develop our understanding of the languages as we progress with this course.
Below we provide information about installing necessary components for each software.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Introduction
R has a long history, dating the early 1980s, and also an ever-growing body of user-contributed add-on packages. It also has an active community providing online support on forums such as Stack Overflow, and a substantial corpus of code online, meaning that large language models will be well suited to support you in your programming in R. It provides you with the large majority of tools you will need throughout this course, as well as the programming environment necessary to extend available tools where required.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Installing and Working with R
Information on how to download R is available on the R website, and further support can be found searching the web. In general, I recommend that you install an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) such as RStudio. RStudio (image below) provides a user-friendly interface for R, allowing you to view any elements that you have generated in the memory in R, output like graphics, help documentation, and so forth. An example of what RStudio looks like is provided below, where you can see that code is visible, as well as graphical output, and information about what is in the your “environment”. For further information on installing RStudio, see the RStudio website. You are of course welcome to use R however you prefer, and you may prefer to edit code in your favourite text editor and execute code from the command line. Throughout the rest of these resources, we will assume that you have R installed on your computer and have some way to interact with it, either via an IDE or some other work flow that suits you.



RStudio screenshot

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Further Resources
From here we will move to a first class about R as a language, and an overview of a number of key elements. If you are interested in generating a more complete overview of R, a number of free resources can be consulted, such as the following books provided free online:

Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund (2023) R for Data Science
Wickham (2016) ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis

Wilke (2019) Fundamentals of Data Visualization: A Primer on Making Informative and Compelling Figures

A range of other textbooks are available that may help you with your work in R including:

Matloff (2011) The Art of R Programming.

and, with a particular focus on economics and causal methods:

Huber (2023) Causal Analysis: Impact Evaluation and Causal Machine Learning with Applications in R.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Python

Introduction
Python was developed in the late 1980s by Guido van Rossum, and is an open source language which has gained considerable traction with users and developers, meaning that a diverse array of packages now exist to expand the base language. Like R, it has an active community providing online support on forums such as Stack Overflow, and a lot of online code available. It provides you with the large majority of tools you will need throughout this course, as well as the programming environment necessary to extend available tools where required. Python has had a number of major version upgrades throughout its history, but now versions 3 and above of Python are widely adopted. I recommend working with some version greater than 3 when you install Python, as code written in version 2 will not necessarily work in version 3.


Installing and Working with Python
Information on how to install Python can be found at the Python website, which has a brief wiki discussing installation on various operating systems. Once you have Python installed in your operating system you could work directly with Python from the command line by typing “Python” and you may see output like the below.

python

Python 3.8.10 (default, May 26 2023, 14:05:08)
[GCC 9.4.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
I recommend that along with Python, you install in Integrated Development Environment (IDE), or simply work with a text editor which provides the capabilities of an IDE. There are many IDEs which can be used with Python, see for example the list here. I can recommend Spyder (see below for a screen shot of what this looks like), or alternatively, might recommend VS Code as a broader editor which offers these capabilities and more. The value of having this IDE is that you can easily view any elements that you have generated in the memory in Python, output like graphics, help documentation, and so forth. An example of what Spyder looks like is provided below, where you can see that code is visible on the left, as well as graphical output, and calls to the command line on the right. You can also display other pieces of information such as documentation and information about what is in the your “environment”. For further information on installing Spyder, see the Spyder website. You are of course welcome to use Python however you prefer, and you may prefer to edit code in your favourite text editor and execute code from the command line. Throughout the rest of these resources, we will assume that you have Python installed on your computer and have some way to interact with it, either via an IDE or some other work flow that suits you.



Spyder screenshot




Further Resources
A number of broader resources are available about Python. A very nice free online text book is:

McKinney (2023) Python for Data Analysis.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Stata

Introduction
Stata was first developed in the mid 1980s, and is now up to release 18. Stata is particularly strong at data manipulation and statistical modelling, and along with their own developers, has an active community of researchers who contribute user-written packages. It also has an active community providing online support on forums such as Stata List. It provides you with the large majority of tools you will need throughout this book, as well as the programming environment necessary to extend available tools where required. Stata releases a new version of the program every couple of years, and a strength of Stata is that it guarantees backwards compatability. Thus, code written in older versions of Stata can be run seamlessly in future versions. However, code written in newer versions of Stata will not necessarily work in older versions of Stata, because in each version of Stata new tools are added.


Installing and Working with Stata
Stata is a paid software, and installation is described when licences are purchased. The installation of Stata is relatively straight-forward provided access is available.
For students at Exeter, Stata is available for free fom the Home Software Hub. Details regarding the process of installing can be found at this page: https://www.exeter.ac.uk/departments/it/new/softwarecatalogue/stata/
When installing Stata, the language comes with its own Graphical User Interface (GUI) which is quite user friendly. This GUI provides a command line to interact with Stata and an output window, as well as a list of commands recently executed. It also has a number of emerging windows including a built in file editor, and a graphics window. An example of what Stata looks like is provided below, where you can see that a code editor is visible, as well as a screen below where one can interact directly with Stata.



Stata




Further Resources
From here we will move to a first tutorial about Stata as a language, and an overview of a number of key elements. If you are interested in generating a more complete overview of Stata, I would highly recommend the list of resources provided on the Stata webpage. At this link they include things such as books and blogs on Stata, but also provide a number of video tutorials and online resources specifically related to learning Stata.

title: Getting Set Up
text:
Other Tools
There are surely a range of other tools that you will want to have in your arsenal, and each person’s optimal “research infrastructure” will be different. As a minimum, doing research well in a computationally demanding environment likely requires the following types of tools, and we will work with many of these throughout the semester:

A code editor (note, this might be bundled with the language you use), or you may prefer something like emacs, VS Code, or so forth which offers broader tools.
A way to write your paper. This may be some typesetting tool like LaTeX
Some way to keep track of changes in versions of your code. Git is the most common tool for this.
Some scientific programming language like the ones discussed above.

There are also a range of other tools which you may use which depending on your work flow. This may include things like bibliography management tools, alternative softwares for typesetting slides or online presentation of papers (including markdown-style options), programmes for optimising communication and workflow in teams (such as slack), some sort of note taking, to do list management, and calendar tool for your, and so forth. Of course the list goes on, and will depend on your own particular needs and wants!
